component.name: Open Audio Analyzer
component.summary: Loudness and spectrum metering for mixing, mastering and delivery

description.p: Open Audio Analyzer is a free and open-source loudness and spectrum analyzer: an arrangeable canvas of meter modules driven by presets, delivery targets and skins.

Loudness follows EBU R 128 and ITU-R BS.1770-4 — momentary, short-term and integrated LUFS, loudness range, and true peak by four-times oversampling — and is held against the EBU Tech 3341 and 3342 conformance vectors on every build. What Open Audio Analyzer has not measured it does not draw: an unavailable quantity is a dash, never a zero.

ul.li: Number Box, LUFS Meter, Digital Meter and Super Meter
VU Meter with a real second-order movement
Spectrum Analyzer, Spectrogram, Phase Scope and Stereo Cloud

description.p: Files can be analysed offline against a delivery target, from the application or from the bundled command-line analyser. A tablet on the same network can mirror the canvas as a second display.

A preset is a document: Open, Save and Save as in a File menu, with the open preset named in the status bar and marked when it differs from the file. The meters no longer freeze when a capture source stops delivering — the engine notices within a quarter of a second, puts the source back where it can, says so on screen, and counts the audio that was missed as lost. The plugin's window is drawn in the application's own palette and shows which of the three places the path can break has.

The name under the application's icon is Audio Analyzer on iPadOS and Android, where it was OAA. Nothing is renamed on the desktop, and the documentation site now states the readings the engine actually took from a real track rather than readings a mock invented.

Skins can be edited in the application. Settings, Appearance, Edit skin opens all thirteen colour roles with a picker on each, prints every role's contrast ratio against the surface it is read on, and repaints the canvas and any tablet mirroring it as a colour is dragged. The two skins that ship can no longer be replaced by a file on disk. Open Audio Analyzer also has a new logo, a white waveform on a teal ramp, and every icon it installs follows it. The VU meter has a face: a scale band along the rim, a needle under a machined hub, a mark that holds the loudest point of the last second and a half, and the reference level that reads as 0 VU printed where it can be seen. The spectrogram and the oscilloscope can be drawn in full colour, off by default, the spectrogram colouring level and the oscilloscope the balance between bass, mids and highs. The loudness distribution fits its axis to the programme instead of always drawing sixty decibels of which fifty are empty, and a menu now marks the value it holds by recessing that row rather than by making it the brightest one. Delivery targets can be reset to the built-in six. No measurement changes in this release.

Two loudness readings change, both found by running the official EBU and ITU vector sets for the first time. Material of 7.1 channels or wider read 0.35 LU too loud, because the surround weight was applied to the rear pair as well as the side pair; and the maximum momentary and short-term loudness are now looked for on a 10 ms grid instead of a 100 ms one, so a transient that fell between the old points reads up to 0.7 LU higher. Integrated loudness, loudness range and both peak readings are unchanged. The spectrum analyser now draws its bands tilted, 4.5 dB per octave by default, which leaves a mix roughly horizontal and spends the height on what deviates from that rather than on the ramp every mix has. The oscilloscope can be triggered by a transient, and carries its height and threshold as sliders on the module itself. The histogram can be smoothed, and the loudness distribution prints its range at last.

A fourteenth meter: an oscilloscope, showing the waveform itself with a lane per channel. Its time base runs from 5 ms to 5 seconds and sets how the window is found as well as how much of it there is — below 200 ms the display is triggered on a rising zero crossing, so a periodic signal stands still and can be read, and above it the display rolls right to left the way a waveform is drawn in an editor. Anything that reached full scale is drawn in the over colour. The meters also no longer lose a measurement to the frame-rate setting: at 30 frames a second they still see everything the engine published, they simply redraw it less often.

The Linux download that carries the VST3 is a tarball: unpack it and run ./install.sh, which needs no root and writes under your home directory unless you ask it for --system. It is its own uninstaller too. This flatpak still installs the application alone, and that is a property of the format rather than something left undone — a plugin built against the sandbox's libraries cannot be loaded by a DAW running on the host's. The Linux VST3 is now built against the same glibc as everything shipped beside it, where being built against a newer one made it absent from an older distribution's plugin browser with nothing logged. A display can also be paired by camera now: the desk shows a QR code and a tablet reads it, which is the route that works on a network that blocks multicast.

The application identifier is now com.openaudioanalyzer.oaa. On Linux that is also the flatpak application id, so this release installs beside an earlier one rather than upgrading it; remove the old dev.openaudioanalyzer.oaa if you do not want both. Downloaded macOS builds no longer need a quarantine flag stripped by hand, because the plugin bundles and the disk image are notarised. The VST3 and Audio Unit are universal and load on macOS 14.2 and later, where every previous release shipped a bundle built only for the machine that built it.

The canvas no longer slows down the longer a spectrogram is on screen: its history is now kept as pixels and drawn as one image, at a fixed cost whatever the signal does. On a remote display the tab control sits beside the name of the machine being watched instead of stranded in the middle of the link bar. On macOS, double-clicking the status bar zooms the window again, obeying the system's title bar setting. The iOS and Android home screen label is now OAA, which a tablet has room to draw.

The macOS VST3 and Audio Unit now carry a valid code signature. Every previous release shipped one that did not verify, which on Apple silicon is enough for a DAW to leave the plugin out of its browser without saying why. The documentation site now says which folder each format has to be copied into, and what a downloaded copy needs before macOS will load it.

Metering your Mac's own output no longer needs a loopback driver: on macOS 14.2 and later, System Output is a Core Audio process tap with nothing to install and nothing to reroute. An Android tablet finds hosts on the network by itself and remembers its layout, its skin and the host it was last attached to. The wire protocol is at version 3, and a display now accepts any version it knows rather than only its own, so a plugin left in a DAW's folder keeps working across an upgrade.

A DAW's playhead now reaches a tablet, and both screens show the host's transport. The desktop accepts the plugin's connection at last, so inserting a VST3 or an AU meters what the DAW is playing. Two readings are corrected and warrant a re-measure: the clip indicator catches clipping it was missing, and crest is taken over the audio rather than off the meters' ballistics.

Thirteen modules that all measure something. Loudness, true peak and the spectrum are held against the EBU R128 and BS.2217 reference vectors in CI. Layouts, delivery targets and skins persist; files are analysed offline; a tablet mirrors the canvas over the network, and a headless VST3 or AU plugin streams a DAW's audio to the desk.
